Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

table.title: Social Curiosity: Study 2 (Circle Slips)
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: Do preschool-aged children seek out information about how others evaluated them? We hypothesize that 3- and 4-year-old children care about how an adult evaluated a tracing of theirs, and deliberately seek out such information. Specifically, we predict that participants who have the chance to view an evaluation of their own tracing will be more likely to "peek" at it than participants who have the chance to view an evaluation of another individual's tracing.
table.design_dependent_variables: After an experimenter evaluates the participant's and another child's (i.e., "Jordan", an unfamiliar, gender-matched child to the participant) tracings, they will leave the experimental room with either the child's or Jordan's evaluated tracing within a folder on a table in front of the participant. The key dependent variable is whether or not children peek at the folder when the experimenter is away.
table.study_design_overview:
Children will be randomly assigned to either the Self condition or Other condition (between-subjects). Children will make a tracing (either of a tree or a bird, counterbalanced) then be shown another unfamiliar child's tracing (either a tree or bird, whichever the child did not trace). The two tracings will be placed inside of separate folders and evaluated out of sight.

After evaluation, the experimenter will leave behind one of the folders on the table in front of the child. The key condition difference is which folder the children were left with: either the one containing their own tracing (Self condition), or the other child's tracing (Other condition). Children will be left alone in the room for a total of three minutes.
table.statistical_tests: We will use a Fisher's Exact Test to test for a condition difference on whether children peeked at the folder during the test phase.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Participants will be excluded for interference (e.g., teachers, children, or other individuals), experimenter error (e.g., large deviations from the study script), failure to complete the study, peeking at the folder prior to the delay phase, having parent-reported developmental delays, or technical errors (e.g., video does not record).
table.sample_size: We plan to run 36 children between the ages of 3;0 to 5;0 (year;month) in each condition (72 total).
table.additional_comments:
As an exploratory analysis, we may test for a condition difference on children's time taken before peeking at the folder within the three minute window. We will code children's peektime as three minutes if they did not peek during the three minute window (as done in previous work, see Kidd et al. (2013)).

We may also explore the effect of age both on our main analysis (proportion of children peeking) and time-to-peek (above).

table.title: Social Curiosity: Study 3 (Forced-Choice)
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: Do preschool-aged children seek out information about how others evaluated them? We hypothesize that 4- and 5-year-old children are more curious to find out how others evaluated their own work versus the work of another child. Specifically, we predict that children would be more likely to look at their own evaluation (rather than another individual's) when given explicit permission to look at either one.
table.design_dependent_variables: After an experimenter evaluates the participant's and another child's (i.e., "Jordan", an unfamiliar, gender-matched child to the participant) tracings out of sight, they will give children permission to look at one of the evaluations. The key dependent measure is which folder children choose to look inside of.
table.study_design_overview:
Single condition experiment. Children will make a tracing (tree or bird; counterbalanced) then be shown another unfamiliar child's tracing (tree or bird, whichever the child did not trace). The two tracings will be placed inside of separate folders and evaluated out of sight (order of evaluation and folder color counterbalanced).

After evaluation, the experimenter will offer for children to look inside of one of the folders to see the evaluation.
table.statistical_tests:
To analyze whether participants' choice of folder differs from chance, we will compute the Bayes Factor test of a single proportion, using the proportionBF command from the BayesFactor package in R (Morey et al., 2024).

i.e., proportionBF(k, n, p = 0.5)

We will use the package default priors: a point distribution at 0.5 representing H0, and a logistic distribution centered at 0 (i.e., log-odds corresponding to 0.5) with the default prior r scale ½ representing H1. 

We will interpret a BF10 > 10 as strong evidence, > 5 as moderate evidence, and > 3 as weak but meaningful evidence in favor of H1. We will use the same thresholds to interpret evidence in favor of the null (i.e., BF01)
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Children will be excluded for interference (e.g., due to teachers, children, or other individuals outside the research room), experimenter error (e.g., large deviations from the study script), looking at one of the folders prior to the key test phase, failing to complete the study, having parent-reported developmental delays, or technical errors (e.g., video does not record).
table.sample_size:
We are uncertain as to the size of the effect we will observe (if any), thus we plan a sequential Bayes Factor analysis (e.g., Mani et al., 2021). We will calculate the Bayes Factor via the analysis plan outlined above.

We will test an initial sample of 20 children (4- and 5-year-olds), then evaluate the Bayes Factor (i.e., BF10) after every 4 data points. We will stop testing at BF10 > 10, BF10 < ⅕, or at an N = 36.
table.additional_comments: For consistency with previous studies in this line of work, we will also conduct a frequentist analysis of the data (Exact Binomial Test) at the conclusion of data collection.

table.title: Social Curiosity: Study 4 (Uncertainty)
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: We hypothesize that 4- and 5-year-old children would be more curious to find out how others evaluated their own work when they are more uncertain about whether they received a positive evaluation. Specifically, we predict that children would be more likely to look at their own evaluation (rather than another individual's) when they completed a novel, difficult task than when they completed a simple task they had done before.
table.design_dependent_variables: After an experimenter evaluates the participant's tracing (either a Line or a Bird, see "Conditions") and another child's (i.e., "Jordan", an unfamiliar, gender-matched child to the participant) tracing out of sight, they will give children permission to look at one of the evaluations. The key dependent measure is which folder children choose to look inside of.
table.study_design_overview:
Children will be randomly assigned to the Line-Line-Line condition, or the Line-Line-Bird condition. First, children across both conditions will receive two rounds of evaluation from the experimenter on two identical line tracings, each time receiving positive evaluation in the form of a star. Then participants will be presented with a final tracing: either the same line tracing (Line-Line-Line condition), or a bird tracing (Line-Line-Bird).

After children complete their final tracing, they will be told that another unfamiliar child made a tracing. The two tracings will be placed inside of separate folders and evaluated out of sight.
table.statistical_tests:
We will run the following Bayesian generalized linear model in the rstanarm (Goodrich et al., 2024) package in order to determine whether folder choice differs by condition:

stan_glm(formula = choice ~ condition,
family = binomial,
data = data)

"Choice" corresponds to the primary dependent measure (i.e., whether children choose their own folder (coded as 1) or Jordan's folder (coded as 0)), and "condition" corresponds to either the Line-Line-Bird condition (coded as 1) or Line-Line-Line condition (coded as 0; between-subjects).

We will use the package default of weakly informative priors (normal distributions on coefficients with SD = 2.5, scaled to predictor magnitudes).

In order to assess the hypothesis of an effect of condition on choice, we will compute the Bayes Factor using the bridgesampling (Gronau et al., 2020) package in R. We will compare a model with a condition term (i.e., choice ~ condition) and one without (i.e., intercept-only model; choice ~ 1;):

bf(conditionterm_model, interceptonly_model)

We will interpret a BF10 > 10 as strong evidence, > 5 as moderate evidence, and > 3 as weak but meaningful evidence for a condition effect. We will use the same thresholds to interpret evidence in favor of the null (i.e., BF01)
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Participants will be excluded for interference (teachers, children, or other individuals), experimenter error (e.g., large deviations from the study script), failure to complete the study, looking inside one of the folders prior to the key test phase, ambiguous or uncode-able choice, having parent-reported developmental delays, significant distraction away from the study, or technical errors (e.g., video does not record).

Finally, participants will be asked comprehension questions throughout the study (a total of four times). In each instance, participants will first be asked a free response question (e.g., "Do you remember what [the star slip] means?"); if they fail this question, they will then be asked a forced-choice question (e.g., "Do you think it means I thought your tracing was really good? Or just okay?"). If participants do not answer the free response question correctly at least once, their data will be excluded from analysis.
table.sample_size:
We are uncertain as to the size of the effect we will observe (if any), thus we plan a sequential Bayes Factor analysis (e.g., Mani et al., 2021). We will calculate the Bayes Factor via model comparison (see "Analyses"): comparing a model with a condition term (i.e., choice ~ condition) and one without (i.e., intercept-only model; choice ~ 1).

We will test an initial sample of 20 children (4- and 5-year-olds) in each condition, then evaluate the Bayes Factor on the hypothesis of an effect of condition on folder choice (i.e., bf(conditionterm_model, interceptonly_model)) after every 4 data points (2 per condition). We will stop testing at BF10 > 10, BF10 < ⅕, or at N = 72 (36/condition).
table.additional_comments: For consistency with previous studies in this line of work, we will also conduct a frequentist analysis of the data (Fisher's Exact Test) at the conclusion of data collection.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

info.title: Young children are curious about what others think about them

text.text: Growing up involves learning about ourselves: Who am I, what can I do, and how can I improve?

Although social feedback from knowledgeable others (e.g., parents, teachers) serves as a critical source of information for learning about the self, little work has examined children's curiosity about this information.

Using both naturalistic information-seeking behaviors and a binary choice measure, the current work investigates whether and when preschool-aged children seek information about what others think about them.

We find that children are more curious about how an adult evaluated their own drawing compared to a drawing made by an unknown peer, while ruling out possible alternative explanations (Experiments 1-3).
Critically, this curiosity was modulated by children's uncertainty about their performance (Experiment 4), suggesting that children's preference for the self reflects genuine information-seeking.
These findings provide evidence for an early-emerging curiosity about what others think about the self.

Decades of research in cognitive development has painted a picture of young children as active, curious learners who construct a rich understanding of the world around them (Gopnik, 2012; Gweon, 2021; L. Schulz, 2012).

Schulz, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, this large body of empirical work on early learning has primarily characterized curiosity as an intrinsic motivation to learn about the world: the physical and social environment that surrounds the learner (Gottlieb, Oudeyer, Lopes, & Baranes, 2013; Jirout, Evans, & Son, 2024; Kidd & Hayden, 2015; Loewenstein, 1994).

text.text: Yet, growing up means far more than learning about the external world; it also means learning about ourselves.
From our strengths and weaknesses to our identity and personality, building a coherent and integrated understanding of the self is a key challenge throughout the lifespan.

As adults, we can easily recall a time when we were curious about ourselves and actively sought out information: We may have attempted a challenge just to see if we could do it, directly asked others for feedback on our work, or even eavesdropped on a conversation if we heard our name.
Such a drive to learn about the self may be particularly important in early childhood, as children tackle new tasks and interact with new people.

While psychology as a field has long recognized that the self may also be a target of learning and reasoning (Bem, 1972; Epstein, 1973; Nisbett & Wilson, 1977), the question of whether young children actively seek information about themselves still remains open.

text.text: Curiosity and information-seeking about the self may manifest in many ways.

Just as children learn about the external world through their own exploration or from others, they might learn about the self through trying something out themselves (e.g., observed successes and failures) or through feedback provided by others.

But especially for young learners, who often lack the expertise to evaluate their performance on their own, social feedback from others can be a particularly powerful source of information about the self.
Specifically for tasks without clear, objective markers for success (e.g., drawing), children often look toward adults for feedback (e.g., "How did I do?").
Yet, these anecdotal behaviors do not provide clear evidence for curiosity about the self.

Given that children, especially in Western cultures, often receive (and may even expect) positive responses from adults (Brummelman, Nelemans, Thomaes, & Orobio de Castro, 2017; Brummelman, Thomaes, Orobio de Castro, Overbeek, & Bushman, 2014), such solicitation may simply reflect children's desire for socially rewarding responses.
text.formatted: Given that children, especially in Western cultures, often receive (and may even expect) positive responses from adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Brummelman, Nelemans, Thomaes, & Orobio de Castro, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Brummelman, Thomaes, Orobio de Castro, Overbeek, & Bushman, 2014)</ref>, such solicitation may simply reflect children's desire for socially rewarding responses.

text.text: Based on prior work, we may entertain at least two possible hypotheses about children's curiosity about what others think about the self.

First, given that praise can serve as positive social reward (Gaines, Duvall, Webster, & Smith, 2005; Webster, Duvall, Gaines, & Smith, 2003), children may only seek such feedback to "feel good" rather than as a source of information; if this is the case, then children's tendency to seek self-relevant feedback may reflect a blanket drive to attain rewarding input.

text.text: Second, it is possible that children treat such feedback as not just positive reward, but also genuinely informative about the self.
If so, this may not only lead children to seek such feedback, but critically, to do so strategically depending on the context.
The current studies aim to adjudicate between these possibilities.
In order for children to be curious about what someone thinks of them and to use it as information to learn about the self, two key cognitive prerequisites must be present.
First, children should be able to represent other agents as capable of evaluating them in the first place.
Indeed, prior work has shown that young children are sensitive to what others think about the self and try to manage such beliefs.

Preschool-aged children can be more likely to cheat at a game if they are praised or told they have a reputation for being "smart" or "good" (e.g., Zhao, Heyman, Chen, & Lee, 2017 , 2018), and they adjust their behaviors when they believe others may be watching them (e.g., to appear more prosocial, fair, or mature; Engelmann, Herrmann, & Tomasello, 2012; Leimgruber, Shaw, Santos, & Olson, 2012; Ma, Zeng, Xu, Compton, & Heyman, 2020).

text.text: By age 4, children even strategically communicate about their competence to revise others' outdated beliefs about them (e.g., Asaba & Gweon, 2022), suggesting that they can represent, and care about, others' beliefs about the self.

text.text: Second, to use others' feedback as a signal for learning, children must be able to consider how and when others' evaluations can be informative about the self.
A body of prior work on mindset development (e.g., Dweck, 2013) has shown that children interpret adults' social feedback as a nuanced signal about the self.

text.text: For instance, praising school-aged children's intelligence, rather than effort, can decrease their motivation when they encounter difficulty (Henderlong & Lepper, 2002; Mueller & Dweck, 1998), suggesting that children are sensitive to how adults' praise bears on different aspects of the self.

text.text: In addition, recent work has shown that preschool-aged children are able to infer the informativeness of an adult's praise based on the adult's past history of being a selective or indiscriminate praiser (Asaba, Stegall, Hembacher, Frank, & Gweon, 2025), suggesting that children also know when particular feedback may be more or less informative about the self (see also Brummelman et al., 2014).

text.text: Taken together, this body of work has shown that the ability to represent and reason about others' evaluative feedback is present even after just a few years of life.

However, these studies often involve situations where children are given explicit feedback or can readily infer what others think about them, leaving open questions about whether children are genuinely curious to learn about themselves and actively seek out self-relevant information from others.

To address this question, we start by gauging children's curiosity about the self against their curiosity about another child: All else being equal, would children be more motivated to find out how an adult evaluated their own performance than a peer's performance?
This contrast allows us to experimentally assess the degree of children's self-curiosity with a well-matched alternative.

text.text: We hypothesized that if children are more curious about how the experimenter evaluated their own work than their peer's work, they might be more tempted to seek this information when left alone.
The key dependent measure was whether the participant peeked inside a folder when the experimenter was out of the room.
Children were randomly assigned to either the Self condition or the Other condition.
In the Introduction Phase, children were instructed to make a drawing; then, they were told that another child, Jordan, also made a drawing.

The experimenter then placed each drawing into a different folder (e.g., the participant's drawing inside a yellow folder, and Jordan's inside a green folder; color counterbalanced) and told participants: "Okay, I am going to the back of the room to take a close look at each of these drawings, and put a star sticker inside the folder if I think it's really good!"
In the Evaluation Phase, the experimenter brought the folders to the back of the room and pretended to evaluate the drawings.
The procedure made it clear to children that the experimenter was evaluating each drawing independently rather than directly comparing the two.

Finally, the experimenter returned to the table and offered to show the participant if the folders contained star stickers, suggesting that they look at one of the two drawings first: either the child's own drawing (in the Self condition) or Jordan's drawing (in the Other condition).
Just as the experimenter was about to open it in front of the child, they received a phone call and had to step outside.
The experimenter exited the room saying, "I'll be right outside if you need me, I'll be back!"

; they left the folder on the table and took the other one with them, leaving the participant alone in the room with their own folder (Self condition) or with Jordan's folder (Other condition) for a total of three minutes.
The experimenter then returned to the room and looked inside both folders with the participant.

In this experimental context, children in either condition were given little incentive to peek; the experimenter clearly intended to open both folders with the child, and left after saying they would be right back, signaling the prospect of looking inside both folders and an implicit agree-ment to wait.
Thus, peeking-a form of information-seeking-would emerge only if the child's curiosity about the experimenter's evaluation was stronger than their desire to wait.
This behavior offered two distinct but complementary dependent measures: (1) whether children peeked inside the folderfoot_0 and (2) if they did, how quickly they did so (peek latency).

text.text: If children are more curious about the experimenter's evaluation about themselves than about Jordan, they should be more likely to peek and be faster to do so in the Self than in the Other condition.

As predicted, children were more likely to peek inside the folder in the Self condition (n = 13/20, 65%) than in the Other condition (n = 5/20, 25%; Fisher's exact test: p = .025, OR = 5.31, 95% CI: [1.19, 27.62]; see Fig. 2).

text.text: To analyze peek latency, we conducted a survival analysis in order to account for the potential of heavily right-censored data (i.e., children who never peek and thus would not have a peek latency).
The survival analysis yielded a significant effect of condition (Mantel-Cox log rank test: p = .015).
We found no evidence of an age effect in either measure (see Materials and Methods).
These findings provide preliminary support for our hypothesis.

text.text: However, it is possible that children in this study treated the star sticker as a form of material reward.

If so, children in the Self condition may have been simply drawn to "their" sticker or become curious about whether they received one, not as a form of positive evaluation but as a tangible, marshmallow-like reward-even though the folders were explicitly described as the experimenter's and there was no indication that children could take the sticker with them (see Materials and Methods).
Experiment 2 was designed to address this possibility.

Experiment 2 (n = 73, 3-and 4-year-olds, preregistered at https://aspredicted.org/f6q2-wm3z.pdf) aimed to provide a replication of Experiment 1 with a younger, narrower age range, while also addressing the concern that Experiment 1 results could be explained simply by the appeal of the gold star sticker.

text.text: Given the absence of an age effect in Experiment 1, we constrained the age range to just 3-and 4-year-old children.
The procedure of Experiment 2 largely followed that of Experiment 1, with two main changes.
First, the gold star stickers were replaced with an arbitrary symbol: square pieces of paper with black printed circles on them.
These black circle slips were unlikely to have any intrinsic value to children or prior association with a reward.
During the Introduction Phase, children were shown the circle slips and told that the experimenter would place one inside the folder if they thought a drawing was "really good."
Second, children completed a tracing task, rather than a free-form drawing task, which we implemented in order to standardize and reduce the time children spent making their drawings.

Overall, we found a pattern of results in Experiment 2 that largely mirrored those in Experi-ment 1.
However, the difference in peeking rates between conditions was attenuated (OR = 5.31 in Experiment 1 vs.
OR = 2.91 in Experiment 2; see Materials and Methods for additional analyses) and the effect was relatively fragile (see Footnote 3).

While this may simply reflect random variability across experiments, it is also possible that the key change in Experiment 2 (i.e., replacing the star sticker with a black circle slip) yielded a smaller effect size.

For instance, the meaning of getting a black circle slip-compared to getting a gold star sticker, a symbol often used to indicate successful or positive performance-may have been too arbitrary and confusing, especially given the younger age range in this experiment.

Another possibility, however, is that some children in Experiment 1 did treat the sticker as a simple tangible reward, and replacing it with the circle slip correspondingly reduced the effect across conditions.
These possibilities are not mutually exclusive, and both would weaken children's desire to peek in the Self condition in Experiment 2 compared to Experiment 1.

Thus, in Experiment 3, we sought to conceptually replicate this effect in 4-and 5-year-olds by using the circle slips again, but with a different dependent measure: a binary choice to peek at their own vs.
Jordan's folder.

While spontaneous peeking provides a naturalistic way to reveal children's desire for self-relevant information, converging evidence using a direct comparison between one's own and Jordan's folder would provide stronger support for our hypothesis.

text.text: The procedure was largely similar to that of Experiment 2, including the use of circle slips.

The critical difference occurred at the end of the Evaluation Phase: once the experimenter evaluated the tracings and returned to the child, children were told they could look in any folder they wanted, but had to choose only one.
Both folders were then placed in front of the child, and they could indicate their choice by pointing to or grabbing one of the folders.

As predicted, children in Experiment 3 showed a strong preference to look in their own folder (n = 27/36, 75%, Bayesian Single Proportion Test: BF10 = 20.56; Exact Binomial Test: p = .004), providing converging evidence that complements children's peeking behaviors in Experiments 1 and 2.

Notably, children continued to exhibit this preference even with the arbitrary marker of positive evaluation (black circle slip), suggesting that the prospect of material reward inside the folders cannot alone explain our results.

Beyond finding converging evidence across different dependent measures, Experiment 3 also helps rule out another alternative explanation for Experiments 1 and 2: Given prior research on children's understanding of ownership and property rights (Nancekivell, Friedman, & Gelman, 2019; Rossano, Rakoczy, & Tomasello, 2011; Shaw, Li, & Olson, 2012), children may have avoided peeking at Jordan's folder simply because they believed they shouldn't peek at someone else's work and its evaluation.

text.text: Given that children in Experiment 3 were given explicit permission to peek at either folder, concerns about ownership cannot alone explain children's preference to look at their own folder over Jordan's.
Collectively, Experiments 1 through 3 show that children preferentially seek self-relevant information about their performance.
These findings cannot be explained by a simple desire for material reward or a resistance to peeking at other people's information.
However, these studies still leave open at least two alternative explanations.
First, the results are consistent with the possibility that children have a blanket preference for self-relevant information regardless of context.

Second, given that children in our sample routinely receive praise from adults, it is possible that children's tendency to peek at their own folder was driven by their desire for a positive social reward (e.g., feeling good from receiving praise) rather than information about themselves.

A hallmark of curiosity as a drive for information-seeking and learning is that it reflects the learner's uncertainty and expected information gain (Gottlieb et al., 2013; Loewenstein, 1994); indeed, prior work suggests that children exhibit more information-seeking behaviors when there is more to be learned about the world (e.g., Kidd et al., 2012; Lapidow & Bonawitz, 2023; L. E. Schulz & Bonawitz, 2007; Stahl & Feigenson, 2015).

text.text: If children's responses in our studies reflect genuine curiosity to learn about the self, they should also be able to modulate their information-seeking behaviors accordingly.
Experiment 4 aims to test this possibility.

In Experiment 4 (n = 72, 4-and 5-year-olds, preregistered at https://aspredicted.org/j845kc.pdf), we sought to test whether children's choice to peek at their own folder is modulated by their uncertainty: If children's preference for peeking inside their own folder reflects genuine information-seeking, they should be more likely to do so when they have performed a difficult task (and are therefore uncertain about their performance) rather than an easy task that they had already completed and received positive feedback on in the past (and are therefore more certain about their performance).
text.formatted: In Experiment 4 (n = 72, 4-and 5-year-olds, preregistered at <ref type="url" target="https://aspredicted.org/j845kc.pdf">https://aspredicted.org/j845kc    .pdf</ref>), we sought to test whether children's choice to peek at their own folder is modulated by their uncertainty: If children's preference for peeking inside their own folder reflects genuine information-seeking, they should be more likely to do so when they have performed a difficult task (and are therefore uncertain about their performance) rather than an easy task that they had already completed and received positive feedback on in the past (and are therefore more certain about their performance).

text.text: To test this hypothesis, Experiment 4 used the same binary choice measure as in Experiment 3 with a few modifications.

First, before being introduced to Jordan and working on the tracing to be placed inside their folder, children completed two identical tracings that were very simple (dotted line) and received a positive evaluation from the experimenter.

Critically, the third tracing differed by condition: Children in the High Uncertainty condition were asked to trace a bird (i.e., a new, difficult task) whereas those in the Low Uncertainty condition were asked to trace the same dotted line they had already completed twice.

The rest of the procedure was similar to that of Experiment 3: The experimenter introduced Jordan, told children that their third tracing and Jordan's tracing would be evaluated, and then gave them a forced choice to look inside their own or Jordan's folder.

Second, given the strong preference for the self in Experiment 3, some changes were made to minimize ceiling effects by increasing the appeal of choosing Jordan's folder: Children never saw the tracing that Jordan made before their final choice, and the experimenter nudged children to choose Jordan's folder by saying, "Jordan said it is okay for other kids to look."
By making both options-peeking at their own vs.
Jordan's folder-reasonably appealing, we could test whether children's choice would differ depending on their third tracing.

Finally, to indicate positive evaluation, we used a paper slip with a star (rather than a black circle) to minimize children's confusion about the arbitrary symbol while retaining the benefit of using a marker of evaluation that is not as intrinsically rewarding as stickers.
Additionally, unlike the previous studies, we also excluded participants who did not remember the meaning of the paper slips (preregistered exclusion criterion, see Materials and Methods).
This design allowed us to test our hypothesis against several alternative explanations.
For instance, if children simply had a blanket preference for self-relevant information, then children would choose their own folder regardless of condition.

Alternatively, if children simply wanted to maximize expected reward and the possibility of "feeling good," then they would be more likely to choose their own folder in the Low Uncertainty condition than in the High Uncertainty condition.
However, if prior results reflect genuine curiosity about the self, children would be more likely to choose their own folder in the High Uncertainty condition than in the Low Uncertainty condition.

Overall, we found a credible effect of condition on folder choice-children were more likely to choose their own folder in the High Uncertainty (bird) condition (n = 21/36, 58%) than in the Low Uncertainty (line) condition (n = 11/36, 31%; Bayesian Logistic Regression: BF10 = 1.76, β = 1.19, 95% CrI: [0.21, 2.18]; Fisher's exact test: p = .032; Fig. 3), 5 suggesting that children's information-seeking was modulated by whether they completed an easy, familiar task with a predictable evaluation (i.e., low uncertainty) or a novel, difficult task with an unknown evaluation (i.e., high uncertainty).

text.text: Unlike Experiments 1-3, which did not show any effects of age, further exploratory analyses revealed that this effect was primarily driven by older children.

While 4-yearolds (n = 36) showed no difference in folder choice across conditions (BF10 = 0.16, β = 0.15, 95% CrI: [-1.46, 1.58]; Fisher's exact test: p > .99), 5-year-olds (n = 36) showed a robust effect of condition on folder choice (BF10 = 19.16, β = 2.38, 95% CrI: [0.84, 4.12]; Fisher's exact test: p = .005).

text.text: Together, the results of Experiment 4 suggest that children's curiosity about the self-at least by age 5-is more than a blanket preference for the self, or a desire to attain praise.
The fact that the condition difference increased with age provides evidence against simple low-level preferences for the more novel and complex bird tracing.
Rather, this pattern is consistent with the possibility that older (but not younger) children strategically decided whether to seek information about the self depending on their uncertainty.
Scholars have long argued that a central goal of development is to learn who we are (e.g., Bowlby, 2010; Erikson, 1963; Piaget, 1954).

text.text: From this perspective, the idea that children learn about themselves may seem like a truism, especially given how often children ask "How did I do?"
or "What do you think?"-questions that appear to reflect a drive to learn about the self.
Yet, this drive has received surprisingly little scientific attention.

text.text: Using binary choice, we again found a preference for the self, ruling out concerns about another child's ownership or privacy (Experiment 3).

Critically, 5-year-old children flexibly chose to seek information about the self versus another child depending on the uncertainty about their performance, suggesting that children's responses reflect genuine curiosity rather than a blanket preference for self-relevant information or a desire to "feel good" by maximizing praise (Experiment 4).
Taken together, these studies provide evidence for an early-emerging curiosity about the self.

While we did not find evidence for an age-related change in Experiments 1-3, exploratory analyses in Experiment 4 revealed a potential developmental change: Children's tendency to choose their own vs. others' folders depending on their uncertainty was clear in 5-year-olds but not in 4-year-olds.
What might explain the difference across age?
It is possible that younger children were more susceptible to the experimenter's nudge to choose the peer's folder, which suppressed their preference for the self in the High Uncertainty condition.

Alternatively, it is also possible that younger children start out with an undifferentiated representation of self-relevant information as a learning signal, and later come to understand that more novel, difficult tasks carry more diagnostic (and thus valuable) information about one's abilities.
These possibilities are not mutually exclusive, and may reflect the development of metacognitive and social reasoning.

More generally, how children's curiosity about the self leads to actual learning gains-the development of selfknowledge and the construction of an abstract understanding of oneself-remains an important goal for future work.

Our experimental tasks were optimized for a particular sociocultural context (Western, relatively high-SES), leveraging the fact that children in our sample were generally familiar with drawing/tracing and with receiving spontaneous feedback from adults on their work.

However, given that there may be substantial cultural differences in the degree to which children anticipate and receive such feedback in their daily lives (e.g., Ng, Pomerantz, & Lam, 2007; Rogoff, Paradise, Arauz, Correa-Chávez, & Angelillo, 2003), children's curiosity about the self may also manifest differently depending on culture.

text.text: From this perspective, our work highlights the need for studies investigating such learning across cultures, as well as for a unified theory of learning that incorporates a drive to learn not only about the world but also about the self.
Relatedly, our tasks constrained children's curiosity about the self to a particular source (i.e., social feedback), target (i.e., abilities and performance), and measure (i.e., peeking).
However, the drive to learn about one's abilities goes far beyond the simple scenarios presented here.

First, even though the current work used peeking as a way to index information-seeking, children may also learn about themselves in a number of ways, including passive observation (e.g., observing their own successes and failures, or recognizing how others behave toward them) and active informationseeking (e.g., trying out a new challenging task, or directly asking for feedback).
Second, while we focus on a domain where others' feedback is critically helpful, self-generated data may play a more central role in other domains.

For instance, prior work in early motor development has studied infants' physical exploration as a function of locomotor skill (e.g., Adolph, Bertenthal, Boker, Goldfield, & Gibson, 1997; Adolph, Eppler, & Gibson, 1993), which some have characterized as a form of attaining information about the self from one's own actions (i.e., one's motor abilities; Gibson, 1988; Rochat, 1998).

text.text: Finally, even though social feedback is a useful source of information to learn about the self, simply knowing how others view us can serve important goals of its own.
For instance, even after substantial learning about our own traits, abilities, moral character, and physical appearance, we may still care about how others judge us in these domains.

Such "social curiosity" about the self-wanting to know what others think of us-may have been present in the current work, and may play an even larger role as children begin to see themselves as a part of a larger social network.
Lastly, our findings also present key challenges for computational theories of curiosity and learning.

Past and current computational efforts to model intrinsic curiosity and motivation (e.g., curiosity-based reinforcement learning) have primarily focused on methods to push agents to explore and learn about their external environment (e.g., Haber, Mrowca, Fei-Fei, & Yamins, 2018; Kim, Sano, De Freitas, Haber, & Yamins, 2020; Oudeyer, Kaplan, & Hafner, 2007).

text.text: However, our studies point toward a more complex kind of learning about the self: Rather than simply knowing whether we can produce a drawing at all, we want to know whether we are good at doing so, what others think about our abilities, and how we compare to others around us.

These cases of representationally rich, socially laden curiosity about oneself will be a key challenge in the attempt to provide a unified description of curiosity that spans both the world and the self.
Forty 3-to 5-year-olds (M age = 4.75, SD age = 0.57, Range: [3.52, 5.97]; 20 girls) were randomly assigned to the Self (n = 20) or to the Other condition (n = 20).
An additional seven children were excluded for experimenter error (n = 5) and for not completing the study (n = 2).
All children were run at a local nursery school.
Children completed their drawings on a blank sheet of paper by using a set of colored pencils presented in a plastic container.
Two standard-sized folders (green and yellow) were used to put the drawings into; a roll of star stickers was also used, and was either placed on the drawing or on the folder.
Two photos of "Jordan" were used (one boy, one girl); the photo shown was gender-matched to the participant.
Jordan made a tree or a bird (whichever the child did not).
A description of the overall study procedure can be found in the main text.
Children were randomly assigned to either the Self condition or the Other condition.
In the Introduction Phase, children were shown a stack of blank white paper and colored pencils.
The experimenter told children that they were going to play a drawing game.

After children completed their drawings, the experimenter took their drawing and casually moved it to one side of the table (on the left side of the table in the Self condition, and the right side of the table in the Other condition).
Children were then shown a photo of "Jordan," who was described as "a kid, just like you!"
The experimenter said that Jordan also made a drawing and showed it to the child.
Jordan's drawing was selected from several premade drawings made to look like it was drawn by a child.
To avoid direct comparison, Jordan's drawing always depicted something the child did not draw (e.g., a tree if the child drew a bird).

Then, the experimenter told participants that the drawings would be evaluated and placed into two different colored folders (yellow or green), adding that participants' drawings would be placed in one folder and Jordan's drawing in the other.

The experimenter told children that the folders belonged to the experimenter ("This is my [green/yellow] folder!"), such that children did not believe that they could take the folder home, and placed each folder on top of the drawing.

The experimenter then said: "Okay, first, I am going to take a real close look at [your/Jordan's] drawing, and if I think [your/Jordan's] drawing is really good, I'm going to put a star sticker on the inside of my folder.
But if I think this drawing is just okay, I won't put a star sticker."
The experimenter then repeated the same line for the other folder.

The yellow folder was always placed on the left side of the table and referred to first, and the green folder was placed on the right side of the table and referred to second (i.e., the participant's drawing was in the yellow folder in the Self condition, and Jordan's drawing was in the yellow folder in the Other condition).
In the Evaluation Phase, the experimenter then went to the back of the room out of sight, and pretended to evaluate the drawings ("Hmm. . . what did I think of Jordan's drawing?

Okay!"

Unbeknownst to the participant, the experimenter placed a star sticker in both folders.
In the Wait Phase, the experimenter returned to the table with the folders and reminded the participant which drawing was inside each folder.
The experimenter then offered to show the participant whether the drawings had a star sticker.

The drawing the experimenter chose to show first differed by condition: either the child's own drawing (Self condition) or Jordan's drawing (Other condition); the folder shown first was always yellow.
The experimenter placed the folder down on the table in front of the child as if to open it, but then received a phone call and had to step outside.
The experimenter said, "I'll be right outside if you need me, I'll be back!"

Thus, the participant was left alone with their own folder in the Self condition, and with Jordan's folder in the Other condition.
After the end of the Wait Phase, the experimenter returned to the room and showed children that they received a star sticker.

Finally, to avoid implying that the star sticker was theirs to take, it was placed onto the folder (which was explicitly described as the experimenter's folder) rather than on the drawing.

The current work represents a step toward filling this gap by empirically investigating the presence and nature of children's curiosity about the self.
Growing up means learning about ourselves: Who am I, what can I do, and what do you think of me?

Just as much as the field of cognitive development has shown children as motivated learners of the external world around them, here, we show that children are also motivated to learn about themselves, and in particular, what others think about them.

By demonstrating the early presence of curiosity about the self, the current work opens up a new area of inquiry to better understand its modulating factors, developmental trajectory, and downstream consequences on learning.
Beyond serving as the engine for the development of self-concept, such self-oriented curiosity can guide how we navigate our social world and build relationships with others.
